item.case_name: Fact piece about a real thing
item.title: Christmas Eve at Biltmore

turns.text: Make an 8-second widescreen history clip of Biltmore House in Asheville on Christmas Eve 1895, when George Vanderbilt first opened it to family and friends. A slow exterior view is enough. Show 'Biltmore House', 'Asheville, North Carolina' and 'December 24, 1895', plus a small 'Historical reconstruction' label. Warm English narration, historically grounded rather than a fantasy castle.

item.tests: Tests geographic, architectural and period accuracy in a historical reconstruction without misrepresenting generated footage as archival evidence.

answer_sheet.Place and historical event: Biltmore House in Asheville, North Carolina, on December 24, 1895, when George Vanderbilt first opened the house to family and friends.
answer_sheet.Required wording: Biltmore House; Asheville, North Carolina; December 24, 1895; Historical reconstruction.
answer_sheet.Visual treatment: A historically grounded, slow exterior view of the actual house's architecture. Lighting and camera angle are your call.
answer_sheet.People: An exterior view without people is fine; no identifiable portrayal of George Vanderbilt is needed.
answer_sheet.Voice and music: Warm English narration stating the occasion; exact wording, voice and any unobtrusive music are your call.

must_haves: The building is recognizable as Biltmore House, with its pale stone French Renaissance-style facade, steep slate roof and distinctive roofline, rather than a generic castle.
The location and date appear exactly as requested and remain readable.
A legible 'Historical reconstruction' label identifies the imagery as a reconstruction.
No modern cars, contemporary clothing, electric holiday string lights or modern visitor signage appear.
English narration identifies the opening to family and friends, not an opening to the general public.

approvals.name: create_video_from_text

style.prompt: Create an 8-second widescreen historical documentary reconstruction, one continuous slow exterior establishing shot of the real Biltmore House in Asheville, North Carolina, at dusk on Christmas Eve December 24, 1895, when George Vanderbilt first opened his home to family and friends. Historically grounded architectural fidelity is essential: the actual immense Richard Morris Hunt-designed French Renaissance Revival limestone country house, recognizable long asymmetrical east entrance facade, steep dark slate roofs, intricate stone dormers, tall clustered masonry chimneys, entrance stair tower, accurately proportioned stone windows and restrained carved detailing. Not a medieval fortress, not a fantasy castle, no invented soaring spires, no magical effects. Eye-level wide view from the approach, gentle very slow forward camera drift, keeping the house fully recognizable. Muted winter grounds, bare deciduous trees, overcast blue-gray evening sky, subtle warm amber interior lamplight glowing through windows. No snowstorm or exaggerated snowy landscape, no modern cars, no modern holiday lights, no modern objects. A very small unobtrusive horse-drawn carriage near the entrance may suggest invited guests; architecture remains the focus. Naturalistic documentary imagery and understated color, not fairy-tale imagery. Render these exact readable titles as stable clean ivory typography over the darker lower left of the image throughout the full shot, with generous margins: first line 'Biltmore House', second line 'Asheville, North Carolina', third line 'December 24, 1895'. In a small but legible separate upper right corner label display 'Historical reconstruction' throughout. Do not add other captions. Audio: warm gentle English-language documentary narration, clear measured delivery by an original narrator voice, not imitating any celebrity, starting promptly and finishing within eight seconds. Say exactly: 'Christmas Eve, eighteen ninety-five. George Vanderbilt welcomes family and friends to Biltmore House.' Faint winter evening ambience beneath narration, no loud music. Present as a reconstruction, never as genuine archival footage.
